items.explanation: The cartoon's joke is that the trusts have literally taken the senators' seats, charging that corporations like Standard Oil and the great railroads controlled legislation through bribery and influence. Option B is wrong because the Senate was not breaking up monopolies in 1889; the Sherman Act came a year later and was weakly enforced. Option C is wrong because American manufacturing was expanding rapidly, not declining. Option D is wrong because the cartoon shows business leaders dominating politics, not avoiding it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The image accuses the trusts of capturing the Senate through money and influence.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Senate took no effective action against monopolies in this era.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. American industry was booming; foreign competition was not the issue.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The cartoon's point is that business leaders were deeply involved in politics.

options: (A) The growing influence of large corporations over the federal government
(B) The Senate's successful efforts to break up industrial monopolies
(C) The decline of American manufacturing in the face of foreign competition
(D) The refusal of business leaders to participate in politics
items.stem: The cartoon most directly criticizes which of the following developments of the Gilded Age?
items.stimulus: An 1889 Puck magazine cartoon titled "Bosses of the Senate" shows the U.S. Senate chamber with the senators' desks occupied by giant bloated figures labeled as steel, oil, and railroad trusts, while tiny senators peer in from the visitors' gallery.

items.explanation: The 1892 Omaha Platform demanded public ownership of railroads, free coinage of silver, and a graduated income tax, all aimed at breaking corporate power over farmers. Option A is wrong because Populists demanded regulation, not laissez-faire. Option B is wrong because high tariffs protected the very manufacturers Populists opposed. Option C is wrong because farmers wanted silver and inflation to ease their debts, not the gold standard.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Populists wanted the government to restrain corporations, not leave them alone.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Tariffs aided industrial trusts, the Populists' chief enemy.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Debt-burdened farmers favored silver coinage to create inflation, not gold.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Railroad nationalization and a graduated income tax were core Omaha Platform demands.

options: (A) Laissez-faire policies leaving railroads and trusts unregulated
(B) Higher tariffs to protect American manufacturers from imports
(C) The gold standard to keep the money supply stable
(D) Government ownership of railroads and a graduated income tax
items.stem: A farmer in 1892 who agreed with the cartoon's criticism of corporate power would most likely have supported which of the following?

items.explanation: The 1980s celebrated entrepreneurship, cut taxes, and rolled back regulation, treating business as the engine of prosperity, which is the reverse of the cartoon's hostility. Options A, C, and D all represent eras of suspicion or regulation of corporate power: muckraking Progressivism, New Deal regulation, and Roosevelt's trust-busting.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Progressives shared the cartoon's suspicion of concentrated corporate power.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The 1980s embraced pro-business policies, the opposite of the cartoon's stance.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The New Deal regulated banks and industry, continuing the anti-monopoly tradition.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Roosevelt's trust prosecutions reflected the same hostility to monopoly.

options: (A) The Progressive Era, when muckrakers exposed corporate abuses
(B) The 1980s, when deregulation and pro-business policies were celebrated
(C) The New Deal, when the federal government regulated banks and industry
(D) The 1900s, when Theodore Roosevelt prosecuted trusts under the Sherman Act
items.stem: The attitude toward big business expressed in the 1889 cartoon differs most sharply from the attitude dominant during which of the following periods?

items.explanation: Muir wrote that lumbermen would never replant what they cut and that only the federal government had the power and permanence to protect the forests, a view that helped inspire the national park and forest system. Option A is wrong because Muir blamed the lumber industry for destroying the forests. Option B is wrong because Muir explicitly said only 'Uncle Sam,' the federal government, could do the job. Option D is wrong because tourism was not Muir's proposed mechanism of protection.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Muir accused lumbermen of destroying forests they would never restore.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Muir argued that only the federal government could protect the forests.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Federal protection was, in Muir's view, the sole reliable guardian of the forests.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Muir did not propose tourism as the means of saving the forests.

options: (A) Leave forest management entirely to the lumber companies
(B) Rely on state governments to buy up threatened woodlands
(C) Place forests under federal protection and control
(D) Encourage tourists to visit so that local businesses would preserve scenery
items.stem: According to Muir, the best way to protect the nation's forests was to
items.stimulus: Paraphrased from John Muir, Our National Parks (1901): Muir argued that only the federal government — "Uncle Sam" — could save the Sierra forests from lumbermen, since private owners would never replant what they cut.

items.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt set aside some 230 million acres of public land, creating national forests, parks, and wildlife refuges under federal management. Option B is wrong because logging and mining continued on public lands under regulation. Option C is wrong because the movement kept lands in federal hands rather than giving them to states. Option D is wrong because no environmental amendment was ever added to the Constitution.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Conservation massively expanded the federally managed public-land system.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Resource extraction continued on public lands; it was regulated, not ended.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Conservationists fought to keep lands federal, not transfer them to states.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No constitutional amendment on the environment was adopted.

options: (A) Growth of the national parks, forests, and wildlife refuges
(B) The end of all logging and mining on public lands
(C) The transfer of federal lands to state governments
(D) A constitutional amendment guaranteeing environmental protection
items.stem: The conservation movement of the early 1900s led most directly to which of the following?

items.explanation: Repealing limits on strip-mining would accelerate the destruction Muir spent his life opposing, so a conservationist would reject it. Options A, B, and C all extend Muir's principle of federal protection of nature: the EPA, clean-air regulation, and wilderness preservation.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The EPA embodies the federal environmental role Muir championed.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Pollution limits continue Muir's defense of nature against industry.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Wilderness preservation is the direct heir of Muir's conservationism.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Removing mining limits contradicts everything Muir advocated.

options: (A) The creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970
(B) The Clean Air Act's limits on industrial pollution
(C) The expansion of the national wilderness preservation system
(D) The repeal of federal limits on strip-mining in the 1970s
items.stem: A supporter of Muir's conservation ideas would likely have favored all of the following later policies EXCEPT

items.explanation: Latin America and the Caribbean absorbed far more American investment than any other region, which was the economic foundation of dollar diplomacy under Taft. Option A is wrong because Europe received less than half the Latin American total. Option C is wrong because Asia's share was small. Option D is wrong because the claim is far too broad and unsupported by the regional totals.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Europe's total was well below Latin America's in this period.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The data show Latin America as the dominant destination for American capital.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Asia received one of the smallest shares shown.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The table gives regional totals, not evidence about colonial status.

options: (A) American investors were primarily interested in rebuilding war-torn Europe
(B) The United States directed its overseas economic power toward Latin America
(C) Asia received the largest share of American foreign investment
(D) American businesses avoided investing in regions under European colonial control
items.stem: The data in the table best support which of the following arguments about American foreign policy in the early 1900s?
items.stimulus: U.S. private investment abroad, circa 1913 (approximate figures, in millions of dollars): Latin America and the Caribbean — 1,600; Canada — 700; Europe — 700; Asia — 250; Africa — 50.

items.explanation: Taft's dollar diplomacy deliberately steered American loans and investments into Latin America and Asia to extend U.S. influence and displace European power. Option A is wrong because the Good Neighbor Policy belongs to the 1930s and rejected intervention. Option B is wrong because the Open Door concerned China, which drew only a small share of investment. Option D is wrong because the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s restricted loans rather than promoting them.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Good Neighbor Policy of the 1930s repudiated intervention, not promoted investment-led influence.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Open Door addressed China, a minor destination in the table.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Dollar diplomacy used American capital as an instrument of foreign influence.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Neutrality Acts banned loans to belligerents; they did not encourage overseas investment.

options: (A) The Good Neighbor Policy's rejection of military intervention in the 1930s
(B) The Open Door notes demanding equal trading rights in China
(C) Dollar diplomacy, using loans to extend U.S. influence
(D) The Neutrality Acts' ban on loans to warring nations
items.stem: The pattern of investment shown in the table was most directly encouraged by which of the following policies?

items.explanation: Railroads, mining, oil, and agriculture together dwarf manufacturing and utilities, showing that American money went into pulling resources out of Latin America and carrying them to market. Option B is wrong because manufacturing was the smallest category shown. Option C is wrong because the data show heavy resource investment. Option D is wrong because railroads at 500 million far exceeded public utilities at 150 million.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The sector totals show capital concentrated on extraction and transportation.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Manufacturing was the smallest investment category in the table.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Mining, oil, and agriculture totals show strong resource interest.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Railroad investment was more than triple the public-utilities figure.

options: (A) American capital concentrated on extracting resources and moving them to market
(B) Manufacturing was the largest single category of American investment in Latin America
(C) American investors showed little interest in Latin American natural resources
(D) Public utilities received more American investment than railroads
items.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data in the table?
items.stimulus: U.S. investment in Latin America by sector, circa 1913 (approximate figures, in millions of dollars): railroads — 500; mining and smelting — 350; agriculture — 300; oil — 250; public utilities — 150; manufacturing — 100.

items.explanation: The cartoon satirizes Lodge's Foreign Relations Committee for bottling up the Treaty of Versailles, the fight that ended with the Senate rejecting the treaty and the League of Nations. Option A is wrong because the cartoon is about foreign policy, not a general return to neutrality. Option B is wrong because army funding was not the issue depicted. Option C is wrong because Prohibition enforcement was a domestic matter unrelated to the image.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The cartoon targets the treaty fight specifically, not neutrality in general.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Peacetime army funding was not the controversy shown.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Prohibition was a domestic issue with no connection to the cartoon.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Lodge led the Senate opposition that killed the treaty and League membership.

options: (A) Whether the United States should return to neutrality in European affairs
(B) Whether Congress should fund a larger peacetime army
(C) Whether Prohibition agents should enforce the Volstead Act
(D) Whether the Senate should approve the treaty and join the League
items.stem: The cartoon best highlights which of the following controversies?
items.stimulus: A 1919 cartoon shows Senator Henry Cabot Lodge wheeling a patient labeled "the peace treaty" out of an operating room marked "Senate Committee on Foreign Relations," while President Wilson pleads at the door.
